entries.sentence: Chickenpox, measles and hand, foot and mouth all cause rashes in children, but their other signs and the advice on getting help differ.
entries.note: Three NHS-based pages describe each illness; rash common to all, differences in other symptoms and advice

entries.sentence: Chickenpox causes itchy spots that become blisters and then scabs, and the NHS says it usually gets better in one to two weeks.
entries.note: Itchy spots to blisters to scabs; usually better after 1 to 2 weeks

entries.sentence: Measles starts with cold-like signs, and a rash usually follows two to four days later.
entries.note: Cold-like symptoms first; rash 2 to 4 days later (blended NHS pages)

entries.sentence: Hand, foot and mouth disease brings mouth ulcers and spots on the hands and feet, and most cases clear up within about seven to ten days.
entries.note: Mouth ulcers, rash on hands and feet; most cases clear within about 7 to 10 days

entries.sentence: For measles, the NHS says to phone the GP or NHS 111 before going in, to avoid spreading it.
entries.note: Call ahead, do not just turn up

entries.sentence: A rash that does not fade under a glass can be a sign of sepsis from meningitis, and the NHS says to call 999 straight away.
entries.note: Non-fading rash may signal sepsis caused by meningitis; call 999

entries.sentence: All three illnesses can cause a rash, so the other symptoms and the pattern of the spots help to tell them apart.
entries.note: Each page lists rash alongside other symptoms; this is a summary link, not a quoted claim

entries.sentence: Chickenpox usually starts with mild flu-like symptoms such as fever, aches and loss of appetite.
entries.note: Mild flu-like symptoms first including fever, aches, loss of appetite

entries.sentence: The rash then forms itchy spots that turn into blisters and then scabs.
entries.note: Itchy spots, blisters, then scabs

entries.sentence: Measles usually starts with cold-like signs, such as a high temperature, a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, a cough, and red, sore, watery eyes.
entries.note: First symptoms listed

entries.sentence: Small white spots may appear inside the mouth.
entries.note: White spots inside mouth mentioned

entries.sentence: The rash usually appears two to four days after the cold-like symptoms began, often on the head or neck first before spreading outwards.
entries.note: Rash 2 to 4 days after; starts on head or neck then spreads

entries.sentence: Hand, foot and mouth disease often begins with a sore throat, fever and reduced appetite.
entries.note: First stage sore throat, fever, reduced appetite

entries.sentence: A few days later come painful mouth ulcers and spots on the hands and feet, which can turn into blisters.
entries.note: Mouth ulcers and rash of spots on hands and feet that can blister

entries.sentence: The NHS says chickenpox is highly infectious and passes on through blister fluid or droplets from the nose and mouth.
entries.note: Highly infectious; contact with blister secretions or respiratory droplets

entries.sentence: A person is usually contagious from about two days before the spots appear until all have formed scabs, which is usually about five days after the spots first appeared.
entries.note: Contagious from 2 days before spots until scabbed, usually 5 days after; NHS Scotland gives 1 to 2 days before

entries.sentence: Measles virus is carried in tiny droplets that come out of the nose and mouth when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes.
entries.note: Droplets from nose and mouth

entries.sentence: The NHS says it is easy to catch by breathing in these droplets.
entries.note: Easily caught by breathing in droplets

entries.sentence: People with measles are infectious from when symptoms start until about four days after the rash first appears.
entries.note: Infectious from symptoms until about 4 days after rash; sources differ on start point

entries.sentence: Hand, foot and mouth disease spreads through coughing, sneezing, poo and fluid from the blisters.
entries.note: Spread routes listed

entries.sentence: A child can catch it more than once, because many different viruses cause it.
entries.note: Can get it more than once; many different viruses

entries.sentence: The NHS says most cases of chickenpox clear up on their own, usually within one to two weeks.
entries.note: Usually better after 1 to 2 weeks without seeing a doctor

entries.sentence: Children are generally advised to stay off school or nursery until the spots have scabbed over.
entries.note: Stay off until scabbed, about 5 days after spots appeared

entries.sentence: With measles, a child is likely to be unwell enough to spend a few days in bed.
entries.note: Likely to need a few days in bed

entries.sentence: It may take about two weeks to be well enough to return to school or nursery.
entries.note: About two weeks to be well enough

entries.sentence: Children cannot go back until four days after the rash started.
entries.note: Exclusion until 4 days after rash started

entries.sentence: Most hand, foot and mouth cases clear up within about seven to ten days, and the mouth ulcers should pass within a week.
entries.note: 7 to 10 days; ulcers within a week

entries.sentence: Antibiotics do not help, because the cause is a virus.
entries.note: Antibiotics do not help as infection is viral

entries.sentence: For chickenpox, the NHS says to get help from NHS 111 or a GP if new spots keep appearing after seven days, or if redness or pain spreads around the blisters.
entries.note: Spread of redness or pain, or new spots after 7 days, warrant prompt contact (blended results)

entries.sentence: A GP or NHS 111 can also advise about signs of dehydration.
entries.note: Signs of dehydration listed as a reason to seek help

entries.sentence: For measles, the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if measles is suspected.
entries.note: Urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if suspected

entries.sentence: It advises phoning first and not walking in, to prevent further spread.
entries.note: Do not go to GP or other healthcare setting without calling ahead

entries.sentence: A baby with a high temperature, breathing difficulty or poor feeding should also be seen urgently.
entries.note: Contact urgently if high temperature, breathing difficulty or poor feeding in a baby

entries.sentence: For hand, foot and mouth disease, the NHS suggests contacting a GP if symptoms get worse or do not improve after seven to ten days.
entries.note: Contact GP if worse or not improving after 7 to 10 days

entries.sentence: Signs of dehydration, such as sunken eyes, drowsiness or no urine for 12 hours, are also reasons to seek help.
entries.note: Dehydration signs listed

entries.sentence: The NHS says a rash that does not fade under a glass can be a sign of sepsis caused by meningitis, and to call 999 straight away.
entries.note: Non-fading rash may be sepsis from meningitis; call 999

entries.sentence: The NHS adds that the rash may not appear at all, so other signs matter too.
entries.note: Rash may not appear; trust instincts

entries.sentence: These include a high temperature, vomiting, a headache, a stiff neck and a dislike of bright lights.
entries.note: Other symptoms listed

entries.sentence: For measles, the NHS lists a seizure, severe breathing difficulty, being unable to stay awake, sudden confusion, a stiff neck or painful light sensitivity as reasons to call 999 or go to A&E.
entries.note: List of 999 or A&E signs in measles advice

entries.sentence: For chickenpox, the NHS lists breathing difficulty, chest pain, a seizure or a rash that does not fade under a glass as signs needing urgent help.
entries.note: Emergency red flags listed in NHS Scotland and NHS pages

entries.sentence: The NHS says pregnant women, newborn babies and people with a weakened immune system are at higher risk from chickenpox.
entries.note: Higher risk groups named

entries.sentence: They are advised to speak to a GP as soon as they are exposed to the virus or develop symptoms, and may need a blood test to check whether they are protected.
entries.note: Speak to GP when exposed or symptomatic; blood test for immunity

entries.sentence: The NHS also says to tell the receptionist that it might be chickenpox before going into a GP practice.
entries.note: Tell the receptionist before going in

entries.sentence: Anyone pregnant who has been in close contact with measles is told to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111.
entries.note: Pregnant and close contact with measles: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111

entries.sentence: The NHS also advises pregnant women with hand, foot and mouth disease to contact their GP.
entries.note: Contact GP if pregnant and infected

entries.sentence: The NHS says the most effective way to protect a child against measles is two doses of the MMR vaccine.
entries.note: Two doses of MMR most effective

entries.sentence: The NHS vaccination pages now describe the MMRV vaccine, which also covers chickenpox, replacing MMR in the schedule.
entries.note: MMRV covers measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox and has replaced MMR in the schedule

entries.sentence: The NHS says older children and adults born on or before 31 December 2019 can still catch up on MMR for free.
entries.note: Catch-up MMR for those born on or before 31 December 2019

entries.sentence: No vaccine is mentioned for hand, foot and mouth disease in the NHS pages found, so hygiene is the main prevention, including handwashing.
entries.note: Wash hands often, avoid sharing towels and cups; no vaccine mentioned
